Title: Discrete Pathophysiology is Uncommon in Patients with Nonspecific Arm Pain.

Journal/Date: The archives of bone and joint surgery (2016)

MeSH Keywords: None listed


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Nonspecific symptoms are common in all areas of medicine. Patients and caregivers can be frustrated when an illness cannot be reduced to a discrete pathophysiological process that corresponds with the symptoms. We therefore asked the following questions: 1) Which demographic factors and psychological comorbidities are associated with change from an initial diagnosis of nonspecific arm pain to eventual identification of discrete pathophysiology that corresponds with symptoms? 2) What is the percentage of patients eventually diagnosed with discrete pathophysiology, what are those pathologies, and do they account for the symptoms?
[METHODS]: We evaluated 634 patients with an isolated diagnosis of nonspecific upper extremity pain to see if discrete pathophysiology was diagnosed on subsequent visits to the same hand surgeon, a different hand surgeon, or any physician within our health system for the same pain.
[RESULTS]: There were too few patients with discrete pathophysiology at follow-up to address the primary study question. Definite discrete pathophysiology that corresponded with the symptoms was identified in subsequent evaluations by the index surgeon in one patient (0.16% of all patients) and cured with surgery (nodular fasciitis). Subsequent doctors identified possible discrete pathophysiology in one patient and speculative pathophysiology in four patients and the index surgeon identified possible discrete pathophysiology in four patients, but the five discrete diagnoses accounted for only a fraction of the symptoms.
[CONCLUSION]: Nonspecific diagnoses are not harmful. Prospective randomized research is merited to determine if nonspecific, descriptive diagnoses are better for patients than specific diagnoses that imply pathophysiology in the absence of discrete verifiable pathophysiology.

Title: The clinical utility of pain classification in non-specific arm pain.

Journal/Date: Manual therapy (2015)

MeSH Keywords: Adult, Algorithms, Arm, Cross-Sectional Studies, Female, Humans, Male, Middle Aged


--- ABSTRACT ---
Mechanisms-based pain classification has received considerable attention recently for its potential use in clinical decision making. A number of algorithms for pain classification have been proposed. Non-specific arm pain (NSAP) is a poorly defined condition, which could benefit from classification according to pain mechanisms to improve treatment selection. This study used three published classification algorithms (hereafter called NeuPSIG, Smart, Schafer) to investigate the frequency of different pain classifications in NSAP and the clinical utility of these systems in assessing NSAP. Forty people with NSAP underwent a clinical examination and quantitative sensory testing. Findings were used to classify participants according to three classification algorithms. Frequency of pain classification including number unclassified was analysed using descriptive statistics. Inter-rater agreement was analysed using kappa coefficients. NSAP was primarily classified as 'unlikely neuropathic pain' using NeuPSIG criteria, 'peripheral neuropathic pain' using the Smart classification and 'peripheral nerve sensitisation' using the Schafer algorithm. Two of the three algorithms allowed classification of all but one participant; up to 45% of participants (n = 18) were categorised as mixed by the Smart classification. Inter-rater agreement was good for the Schafer algorithm (к = 0.78) and moderate for the Smart classification (к = 0.40). A kappa value was unattainable for the NeuPSIG algorithm but agreement was high. Pain classification was achievable with high inter-rater agreement for two of the three algorithms assessed. The Smart classification may be useful but requires further direction regarding the use of clinical criteria included. The impact of adding a pain classification to clinical assessment on patient outcomes needs to be evaluated.

Journal/Date: Journal of neuroengineering and rehabilitation (2008)

--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: The pathophysiology of non-specific arm pain (NSAP) is unclear and the diagnosis is made by excluding other specific upper limb pathologies, such as lateral epicondylitis or cervical radiculopathy. The purpose of this study was to determine: (i) if the quantitative parameters related to motor unit potential morphology and/or motor unit firing patterns derived from electromyographic (EMG) signals detected from an affected muscle of patients with NSAP are different from those detected in the same muscle of individuals with lateral epicondylitis (LE) and/or control subjects and (ii) if the quantitative EMG parameters suggest that the underlying pathophysiology in NSAP is either myopathic or neuropathic in nature.
[METHODS]: Sixteen subjects with NSAP, 11 subjects with LE, eight subjects deemed to be at-risk for developing a repetitive strain injury, and 37 control subjects participated. A quantitative electromyography evaluation was completed using decomposition-based quantitative electromyography (DQEMG). Needle- and surface-detected EMG signals were collected during low-level isometric contractions of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) muscle. DQEMG was used to extract needle-detected motor unit potential trains (MUPTs), and needle-detected motor unit potential (MUP) and surface detected motor unit potential (SMUP) morphology and motor unit (MU) firing rates were compared among the four groups using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Post hoc analyses were performed using Tukey's pairwise comparisons.
[RESULTS]: Significant group differences were found for all MUP variables and for MU firing rate (p < 0.006). The post-hoc analyses revealed that patients with NSAP had smaller MUP amplitude and SMUP amplitude and area compared to the control and LE groups (p < 0.006). MUP duration and AAR values were significantly larger in the NSAP, LE and at-risk groups compared to the control group (p < 0.006); while MUP amplitude, duration and AAR values were smaller in the NSAP compared to the LE group. SMUP duration was significantly shorter in the NSAP group compared to the control group (p < 0.006). NSAP, LE and at-risk subjects had lower mean MU firing rates than the control subjects (p < 0.006).
[CONCLUSION]: The size-related parameters suggest that the NSAP group had significantly smaller MUPs and SMUPs than the control and LE subjects. Smaller MUPs and SMUPs may be indicative of muscle fiber atrophy and/or loss. A prospective study is needed to confirm any causal relationship between smaller MUPs and SMUPs and NSAP as found in this work.

key_findings.finding: The strongest direct cohort evidence supports that discrete, symptom-corresponding pathology is very uncommon after an initial diagnosis of nonspecific upper-extremity pain: among 634 patients followed within one health system, only 1 (0.16%) had definite discrete pathophysiology identified by the index surgeon and cured surgically; additional possible/speculative diagnoses accounted for only a fraction of symptoms. The study was retrospective and follow-up was limited to subsequent care within that system, and the authors note too few definite cases for the planned primary analysis.

source_tools.relevance: Direct 634-patient follow-up study and exact proportion

key_findings.finding: The clinical construct of nonspecific arm pain is explicitly defined in review literature by absence of objective physical findings and lack of correspondence between symptoms and objective pathophysiology; it is commonly activity/work-related. This supports 'no discrete pathology' as the defining clinical category, while not proving that all symptoms lack biological mechanisms.

In a community diagnostic-examination study, 1,197 adults with arm or neck pain were classified using a structured schedule; 250 had one or more of 11 specific upper-limb disorders, whereas 176 had only nonspecific arm pain. Thus, within this selected examined symptomatic group, nonspecific pain was about 41% of the reported specific-versus-only-nonspecific comparison (176/[250+176]), although this is not a prevalence estimate for all arm-pain patients and the abstract does not provide the full denominator distribution.

source_tools.relevance: Community sample, structured diagnostic framework, and counts of specific vs nonspecific cases

key_findings.finding: A Level II diagnostic study comparing 41 nonspecific with 40 specific arm-pain patients treated 'nonspecific' as medically unexplained/idiopathic and 'specific' as discrete/verifiable. It found more somatoform, PTSD, and panic screening positives in the nonspecific group, but it was a small, likely specialist-based comparative sample and does not estimate the proportion of all arm-pain patients without structural disease.

source_tools.relevance: Operational definitions, population size, and limitations implied by study design

key_findings.finding: Mechanism-focused studies do not establish a single discrete structural, neurologic, or vascular lesion in NSAP. In 40 office workers with NSAP, sensory testing found a spectrum without a dominant phenotype; in another 40-person study, classifications varied by algorithm, with NeuPSIG primarily labeling pain unlikely neuropathic, Smart primarily peripheral neuropathic, and up to 45% classified as mixed. These findings suggest heterogeneity and possible sensitization mechanisms, not a verifiable lesion, and are limited by small cross-sectional samples and unvalidated/partly discordant classification systems.

A small EMG study (16 NSAP participants, 11 lateral-epicondylitis participants, 37 controls) found smaller motor-unit potentials in NSAP, potentially indicating muscle-fiber atrophy or loss, but explicitly concluded that prospective research was needed to establish causality. This is evidence of a possible physiological correlate, not evidence that most patients have a discrete diagnosable myopathy or neuropathy.

source_tools.relevance: Objective physiological testing and explicit causality limitation

key_findings.finding: Diagnostic frameworks emphasize excluding specific mimics rather than assigning a single cause: cervical radiculopathy and focal upper-limb disorders are common comparators, while visceral referral to the elbow/hand is described as extremely rare; red-flag history, examination, and referral are recommended to detect conditions outside routine musculoskeletal care. The available searches did not identify a robust arm-pain cohort quantifying vascular diagnoses specifically, so the evidence is insufficient to give a reliable vascular proportion.

source_tools.relevance: NSAP diagnosed by exclusion of focal upper-limb pathology and cervical radiculopathy
